# Affine rate slices: nested convex geometry and a weighted surface-tail theorem

This is a rate-sensitive restriction on the logarithmic boundary mechanism. For one affine parameter on one moving convex fiber, the inverse-volume defect conditioned on almost every positive exponential rate is a log-concave measure on the zero face. In fact it retains the stronger positive measure-concavity exponent 1/(d-1). The conditional measures decrease as the rate increases. The corresponding surface statement concerns a radially weighted tail with an essential reciprocal-rate factor. The raw surface defect, and even its restriction to one rate, need not have convex support.

No deepestness or physical stationarity is needed for the slice theorem. No Gamma bound or exclusion of defects follows. General finite-PL source labels are deliberately not substituted for geometric affine slices.

## 1. Precise one-fiber hypotheses and conclusion

Let d>=2. Let positive compact convex bodies K_j converge in Hausdorff distance to a positive compact convex body K in R^d. They lie in a fixed ball. Let

    L_j(X)=a_j+c_j.X>0 on K_j,
    (a_j,c_j)->(a,c),  L(X)=a+c.X>=0 on K,
    F=K intersect {L=0} nonempty,  c!=0.

Let M_j->M>0 be normalization constants and lambda_j decrease to zero. Assume

    integral_(K_j) 1/(M_j L_j) dX <= C_inv.           (1)

Use the actual rate r_j=lambda_j(-log L_j)_+. A common compact bound on r_j may be imposed, as in the exponential-floor theorem, but local statements away from rate zero do not need it. Take any joint weak limit, on compact positive-rate intervals, of

    [1_(K_j)dX/(M_j L_j)] delta_(r_j(X)).             (2)

After passage to a subsequence, its restriction to r>0 is

    gamma_r(dX) dr.                                  (3)

There is a version of gamma_r with the following properties:

* gamma_r is a finite measure supported on F, locally bounded in mass for r>0;
* gamma_s>=gamma_r as measures whenever 0<s<r, after choosing the monotone right-continuous version;
* for almost every r>0, gamma_r is 1/(d-1)-concave on compact sets of positive gamma_r-mass, and in particular is log-concave;
* the supports of the nonzero gamma_r are convex and nested, up to the immaterial exceptional rates in the disintegration.

Here positive measure-concavity means, for compact A,B with positive mass and 0<theta<1,

    gamma_r(theta A+(1-theta)B)^(1/(d-1))
      >=theta gamma_r(A)^(1/(d-1))
          +(1-theta)gamma_r(B)^(1/(d-1)).             (4)

The positive-mass qualification in (4) is essential. The log-concave inequality has its usual geometric right side and also holds when either mass is zero. A limiting gamma_r may live in a lower-dimensional subset of F or be an atom. No full-dimensional density on F is asserted.

If the whole joint limit includes rate zero, (3) describes only its positive-rate restriction. It does not remove a zero-rate boundary atom or replace the ordinary inverse density at rate zero.

## 2. Exact anchor projection makes the slices nested

Choose o in int K. For all sufficiently large j, o lies in int K_j and

    b_j=L_j(o)>=b_*>0.

Put n_j=c_j/|c_j|, n=c/|c|, and let R_j be orthogonal maps converging to the identity with R_j n=n_j. Let E=n-perp and q_j=-a_j c_j/|c_j|^2. The level set L_j=s is parametrized by

    X=q_j+R_j y+(s/|c_j|)n_j,  y in E.

Define its compact convex slice D_j(s) in E. Write the anchor as

    o=q_j+R_j o_j+(b_j/|c_j|)n_j.

For 0<s<t<b_j, convexity gives

    D_j(t) contains alpha D_j(s)+(1-alpha)o_j,
    alpha=(b_j-t)/(b_j-s).                           (5)

This statement includes an empty lower slice. Project the slice onto the zero plane along rays from o:

    Dtilde_j(s)=o_j+[b_j/(b_j-s)](D_j(s)-o_j).        (6)

Multiplying (5) by the factor in (6) gives the exact inclusion

    Dtilde_j(s) subset Dtilde_j(t),  0<s<t<b_j.       (7)

Thus the projected convex slices shrink as the rate r increases, since the level corresponding to a positive rate is

    s_j(r)=exp(-r/lambda_j).

This is projection along the anchor, not ordinary orthogonal projection of an arbitrary sublevel collar. It is the normalization needed for exact nesting.

## 3. Coarea, local bounds, and measure-valued Helly convergence

Let m=d-1. Coarea and ds/s=-dr/lambda_j give the exact positive-rate disintegration of (2), in the coordinates above:

    gamma_j(r)= [1/(M_j lambda_j |c_j|)]
                     1_(D_j(s_j(r))) dy.             (8)

The associated projected measures are

    gammatilde_j(r)= [1/(M_j lambda_j |c_j|)]
                     1_(Dtilde_j(s_j(r))) dy.         (9)

On every compact rate interval bounded away from zero, these are decreasing positive measures by (7). Their supports lie in a fixed compact tangential set. For r>=r_0>0, the projection factor in (6) is 1+O(exp(-r_0/lambda_j)), uniformly. In particular, for large j it is at most 2 on r>=r_0/2. Consequently

    gammatilde_j(r_0)(E)
      <= (2/r_0) integral_(r_0/2)^(r_0)
                                 gammatilde_j(r)(E)dr
      <= 2^(m+1) C_inv/r_0.                          (10)

The same bound holds for all larger rates. It gives local uniform domination in r, not merely a bound on an integrated rate law.

For a countable uniformly dense set of nonnegative continuous tangential tests, their integrals against (9) are bounded decreasing functions of r. Helly selection and a diagonal subsequence give convergence at all r outside the union of their countable jump sets. At those rates, the bounds in (10) extend the limits to every continuous test; positivity yields a finite measure gamma_r. Monotonicity passes to the limit. Right limits provide a decreasing right-continuous version without changing the a.e. disintegration.

The projection in (6) moves points by O(exp(-r_0/lambda_j)) on the common bounded supports and changes volume by 1+O(exp(-r_0/lambda_j)). Thus (8) and (9), transported back into physical space, have the same weak limits at the convergence rates. For a continuous test on a compact physical-position/rate product, (10) and dominated convergence identify the limiting joint measure as (3). Every point in a slice with fixed r>0 has L_j=exp(-r/lambda_j)->0. Hausdorff convergence therefore places gamma_r on F.

This argument proves absolute continuity in the positive rate coordinate directly from actual slices. It does not assume a density disintegration in advance or apply a weak-limit claim to arbitrary conditional measures.

## 4. Concavity survives the collapsing slice dimensions

Each measure (9) is a positive scalar times m-dimensional Lebesgue measure restricted to a convex set. Brunn--Minkowski therefore proves (4) for that measure: apply it to A intersect Dtilde_j and B intersect Dtilde_j, whose Minkowski combination lies in the relevant target set intersect Dtilde_j.

For completeness the needed weak-closure argument does not require a density on the limiting face. Suppose mu_j converge weakly to mu on a common compact set and satisfy (4). Given compact A,B with positive mu-mass, use their open epsilon-neighborhoods. For sufficiently large j those neighborhoods have positive mu_j-mass. Their weighted sum lies in the closed 2epsilon-neighborhood of theta A+(1-theta)B. The lower Portmanteau bound on the two open inputs and the upper Portmanteau bound on the closed target imply the desired inequality with this enlarged target and with mu(A),mu(B) on the right. Let epsilon decrease to zero. This proves (4) for mu.

Applying this at the convergence rates from Section 3 proves the assertion. Weighted arithmetic-geometric mean turns (4) into log-concavity. Positive mass in neighborhoods of any two support points then gives positive mass near their strict combinations, so the support is convex. The measure ordering in Section 3 gives the nesting of supports.

The exponent m=d-1 belongs to the original slice dimension. No claim is made that the limit is uniform on its support, or that a density with respect to Hausdorff measure on F has an incorrectly inherited exponent.

## 5. The precise surface consequence retains 1/R

Assume in addition the surface-log compactness and flux hypotheses of `candidate d3b1d852e0e3ae4b`. Let bhat(dn,dX,dR) be the positive logarithmic surface defect with its rate retained, and let zetahat be the inverse defect. In the one-affine setting there is one continuous plane gradient. Choose the same interior anchor o and put

    h(n,X)=n.(X-o)>0,  b=L(o)>0.

The root uniform-rate kernel reads

    M b zetahat(dX,dr)
      = integral Uniform[0,R](dr) h(n,X)
                                      bhat(dn,dX,dR). (11)

Here Uniform[0,0] means the atom at zero. On r>0, (3) and (11) give, for a.e. r,

    integral_(R>=r) [h(n,X)/R] bhat(dn,dX,dR)
                        =M b gamma_r(dX).            (12)

Therefore this particular weighted surface tail is 1/(d-1)-concave and log-concave tangentially, and decreases as r increases. The radial weight, reciprocal-rate factor, and integration over all R>=r are part of the statement. Removing any of them is not justified by the argument. No positive split of bhat into arbitrary source or parameter labels is used.

## 6. Exact two-rate calibration and a necessary limitation

Use Section 8 of `candidate 9a1deed5372bf5ee`. In dimension three let I=[1/3,2/3], t=x+y, and

    K_j={0<=s<=1, x,y>=0:
                       1/j+exp(-j)dist(s,I)<=t<=1},
    L_j=c_j[t-1/j+exp(-2j)],
    c_j->c=exp(1/2), M_j->1/2.

There is one exact affine contact row, whose mark converges to (1/2,3/28,3/28), with marked value 3c/14 and a uniform source core. It is not asserted deepest or physically stationary.

Choose lambda_j=rho/j, with fixed rho>0. The rate-resolved surface defect is

    bhat=sqrt(2) 1_([0,1] minus I) ds delta_(R=rho)
             +2sqrt(2) 1_I ds delta_(R=2rho),         (13)

at X=(s,0,0), n=(0,-1,-1)/sqrt(2). The coarea calculation yields

    gamma_r(ds)=2/(c rho) ds on [0,1], 0<r<rho;
    gamma_r(ds)=2/(c rho) ds on I,     rho<r<2rho;
    gamma_r=0,                       r>2rho.         (14)

For example rho=1/4 keeps all rates in [0,1/2]. Formula (14) can be checked directly: at fixed r, the slice satisfies

    exp(-j)dist(s,I)<=exp(-rj/rho)/c_j-exp(-2j),
    t=1/j-exp(-2j)+exp(-rj/rho)/c_j.

The allowed tangential intervals tend to [0,1], I, or the empty set in the three respective regimes, and t/lambda_j->1/rho. The factor 1/(M_j c_j) tends to 2/c. Thus the inverse measure on each regime is exactly (14), with no surface-kernel inference needed.

Both conditional inverse measures in (14) are uniform on nested intervals, as the theorem requires. Their integral over rates is (2/c)(1+1_I)ds, which is not log-concave. More sharply, the surface measure at rate R=rho has disconnected support [0,1/3] union [2/3,1]. Hence even conditioning the SURFACE defect on one exact rate does not force convex tangential support. The weighted tail in (12) repairs this: the factor 2 on I in (13) is divided by its rate 2rho, producing a uniform density on the full interval below rho.

For an anchor o=(1/2,1/3,1/3), h=sqrt(2)/3 on this zero edge and b=2c/3. Then M b=c/3. Both sides of (12) are 2/(3rho) times uniform measure on the relevant interval. This checks all radial and normalization constants.

## 7. Finite-PL scope and arbitrary allocation labels

For L_j=min_i A_ij, an individual geometric active cell

    C_ij=K_j intersect {A_ij<=A_kj for every k}

is convex. The proof applies to its A_ij-level slices if that same cell in that same sampled fiber has a fixed positive-height anchor (or a uniformly controlled convergent sequence of such anchors). The restricted inverse measure has the required bound because it is part of the total. Tied identical planes can be merged; positive-volume ties of distinct continuous affine functions cannot occur within a fiber. Overlaps on lower-dimensional seams do not affect coarea at a.e. positive level.

However the hypotheses on an exact source allocation do not automatically provide this cellwise anchor in every target fiber. Moreover a source row can split one affine cell by an arbitrary nonnegative density q_i. Such a labeled slice is not uniform on a convex set. The theorem consequently makes no labelwise concavity assertion for general volume martingale allocations.

A concrete illustration is to split the one-affine calibration's inverse measure into the tangential set [0,1/4] union [3/4,1] and its complement. Let each row be its normalized inverse restriction and take its own barycenter as source. Since L_j is globally affine, these are exact L_j-contact rows; their original reweightings partition uniform volume exactly. Both row means remain uniformly interior because each restriction has a positive ordinary-volume component and tangential mean 1/2. At rates 0<r<rho the first row's conditional defect is supported on the two separated outer intervals. Thus arbitrary source labels really can destroy the slice concavity proved for the full geometric affine slice. No deepestness or physical cap stress is claimed for this illustration.

The new retained information is therefore precise: one affine geometry gives nested concave positive-rate inverse slices, or equivalently the radially compensated surface tails (12). General PL geometry requires actual cell anchors, and general source labels cannot replace those cells.

## 8. Finite geometric cells: delayed starts and their exact compensation

There is a bounded extension which explicitly retains cells without a fixed positive-height anchor. Assume a fixed finite presentation

    L_j=min_(1<=i<=k) A_ij,
    A_ij=a_ij+c_ij.X -> A_i,

uniformly in coefficients, with all the positive-body, inverse-mass and compact-rate hypotheses above. Assume the limiting L is not identically zero; in fact inverse-mass boundedness and Fatou imply that L is positive in int K. Use the geometric active cells

    C_ij=K_j intersect {A_ij<=A_lj for every l}.

Merge planes that are identical on the fiber at a fixed index, and pass to a subsequence with a fixed such pattern. The remaining distinct planes have cells with only volume-null overlaps. Empty and lower-dimensional cells contribute zero volume and may be discarded. The cells are not source allocation rows.

For each remaining cell choose o_ij attaining

    b_ij=max_(C_ij) A_ij>0,
    R_i=lim_j lambda_j(-log b_ij)_+ in [0,R_*],        (15)

after another subsequence. This anchor may approach the boundary and its height may tend to zero. If a limiting plane has zero continuous gradient, it is a positive constant: A_i>=L on K rules out a zero or negative constant. Such a plane contributes no positive-rate defect. We therefore retain only cells with |c_ij| bounded below.

Below the threshold R_i, the cell has no rate mass on compact subintervals for all large j. Indeed r<R_i implies exp(-r/lambda_j)>b_ij. For any compact interval of rates strictly above R_i,

    exp(-r/lambda_j)/b_ij ->0 uniformly.              (16)

Project each slice along o_ij onto A_ij=0, exactly as in (6). Convexity and maximality of b_ij give the same exact nesting for levels below b_ij; no interiority of the anchor was used in (5). Equation (16) makes this projection uniformly close to the identity. Integrating over an interval between R_i and a prescribed r_0>R_i gives the analogue of (10). The argument of Sections 3--4 therefore proves that the geometric cell's joint positive-rate limit has, on (R_i,infinity), a decreasing 1/(d-1)-concave conditional measure

    gamma_i(r),  r>R_i.                              (17)

Its support lies in K intersect {A_i=L=0}. Below R_i this measure is zero. Purely from this slicing argument, mass at the threshold R_i has not been excluded. A geometrically collapsing cell can have all its levels in an exponentially thin rate band. This is the precise distinction from a persistent-height cell, for which R_i=0 and the theorem applies at every positive rate.

Now impose the already proved radial uniform-rate identity for the FULL finite-PL parameter, using these geometric cells to express its a.e. gradient. This requires the same surface-log compactness and ordinary logarithmic trace hypotheses as Section 5. It does not require that the cells be source rows. With a fixed inball anchor o, every

    b_i=A_i(o)>=L(o)>0.

Gauss--Green, or the root kernel proof with the gradient identity partitioned by active cells, gives

    V=M sum_i b_i zetahat_i
       = integral Uniform[0,R] B(dX,dR),
    B=projection_(X,R)[n.(X-o) bhat].                (18)

All terms here are positive. Consequently each geometric cell has no atom at a positive rate, even at its threshold R_i>0. Its entire positive-rate law is (17), extended by zero for r<R_i. The total density

    F(r)=M sum_i b_i gamma_i(r)                      (19)

is decreasing as a measure, by the right side of (18). In contrast, an individual delayed cell is zero before R_i and can start positively afterward.

This gives an exact compensation constraint at every positive threshold R. One-sided weak limits exist and are finite: local boundedness of the decreasing F and b_i>0 bound each gamma_i, and each is decreasing after its own start. Subtract the two limits of (19) at R to obtain

    sum_(R_i=R) b_i gamma_i(R+)
      <= sum_(R_i<R) b_i[gamma_i(R-)-gamma_i(R+)]     (20)

as positive measures on physical space. Thus any new cell contribution must be paid for, at the SAME physical locations, by downward jumps in already active cells' weighted conditional measures. In particular a strictly positive smallest threshold cannot initiate the entire positive-rate law if no cell already active below it has a nonzero tail.

Equation (20) does not say that delayed cells are impossible. Jumps in persistent cells can compensate them. Nor does it provide a positive boundary split by geometric plane or by source gradient: only the full B in (18) is used. Distinct source allocations within these geometric cells may still have the disconnected conditional laws from Section 7.

The accompanying exact checker is `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_affine_rate_slice_concavity_defect_transport.py`; it checks the projection identity, the coarea factor, and every constant and rate moment in the two-rate calibration. The convergence and measure-concavity arguments are the analytic proofs above.
